_note: v0.6 Studio tools. A tool is a small group of fields that compiles into (a) plain-English lines Claude reads, (b) words appended to the IMAGE prompt, and (c) claw-gen CLI flags. Data only — the compiler is renderer/tools.js and is pure, so tests/tools.js can exercise every rule with no DOM. Adding a tool is editing this file; nothing else needs to change. Overridable wholesale by a same-named file in userData/presets/.

_schema.id: stable, kebab-case, referenced by categories' auto lists
_schema.group: geometry | fit | making | look — the section it appears under in the Tools menu
_schema.auto: category ids that switch this tool on automatically; '*' means every category
_schema.targets: which pipeline tracks offer it; omit for all three
_schema.fields: kind is number | text | choice | toggle. Nothing is ever required.
_schema.lines: prepended to what Claude reads. FIRST MATCHING RULE WINS, so order most-specific first.
_schema.imageWords: appended to the image-generation prompt only. ALL matching rules apply.
_schema.flags: claw-gen flags, keyed by action. ALL matching rules apply.
_schema.when: field ids that must all have a value for the rule to fire; [] means 'whenever the tool is on'

tools.label: Dimensions
tools.hint: Exact millimetres. The single biggest jump in accuracy.

lines.text: SIZE: {x} × {y} × {z} mm, measured {ref}. These numbers are contractual — expose them as named variables at the top of the file and do not round them to nicer values.
SIZE: {x} × {y} × {z} mm (outside). These numbers are contractual — expose them as named variables at the top of the file and do not round them.
FOOTPRINT: {x} × {y} mm. Contractual; expose both as variables.
SIZE: {x} mm across × {z} mm tall. Contractual; expose both as variables.
HEIGHT: {z} mm. Contractual; expose it as a variable.
WIDTH: {x} mm. Contractual; expose it as a variable.

tools.label: Hardware
tools.hint: Screws, inserts, nut traps — sized from the tables, never from memory.

lines.text: HARDWARE: {count} × {thread}, {method}. Take every diameter, pitch, insert bore and clearance from the FITS SCREWS AND PARTS tables — never from memory, never rounded. State in a comment which table row each number came from.
HARDWARE: {thread}, {method}. Take every diameter, pitch, insert bore and clearance from the FITS SCREWS AND PARTS tables — never from memory, never rounded.
HARDWARE: {thread}. Take the diameter and clearance from the FITS SCREWS AND PARTS tables, not from memory.
HARDWARE: fixed by {method}. Size the feature from the FITS SCREWS AND PARTS tables.

tools.label: Fit & tolerance
tools.hint: How tight it should be on the thing it mates with.

lines.text: FIT: mates with {mates}; should feel like a {fit}; use {gap} mm clearance on the mating face. Put the clearance in its own variable so it can be reprinted tighter or looser without touching the geometry.
FIT: mates with {mates}; should feel like a {fit}. Choose the clearance for that feel on an FDM printer, put it in its own named variable, and say in a comment what value you chose and why.
FIT: mates with {mates}; {gap} mm clearance on the mating face, as a named variable.
FIT: {fit}, {gap} mm clearance, as a named variable.
FIT: this has to mate with {mates}. Leave printer clearance on that face and expose it as a variable.
FIT: it should feel like a {fit}. Pick the clearance for that, as a named variable, and say what you chose.
FIT: {gap} mm clearance on every mating face, as a named variable.

tools.label: Mounting
tools.hint: How it attaches to the world.

lines.text: MOUNTING: {style}, hole pattern {spacing} mm, countersunk so the heads finish flush or below the surface. Expose the pattern as variables.
MOUNTING: {style}, hole pattern {spacing} mm. Expose the pattern as variables.
MOUNTING: {style}, countersunk so the heads finish flush or below the surface.
MOUNTING: {style}. Design the mounting feature for that specifically, not a generic tab.
MOUNTING: hole pattern {spacing} mm, exposed as variables.

tools.label: The part it replaces
tools.hint: What broke, and the numbers you measured off it.

lines.text: REPLACES: a part from {what}. Measured {measured} (measured with {confidence}). Treat callipered numbers as exact and ruler/photo numbers as ±0.5 mm — where a number is uncertain, expose it as a variable and add a one-line comment saying to reprint after checking that dimension.
REPLACES: a part from {what}. Measured {measured}. Expose every measured number as a named variable so a bad measurement is a one-line fix.
MEASURED OFF THE BROKEN PART: {measured}. Expose each of these as a named variable.
REPLACES: a part from {what}.

tools.label: Text & engraving
tools.hint: Lettering that survives a 0.4 mm nozzle.

lines.text: TEXT: "{text}", {mode}, on the {where}, {depth} mm deep. Keep every stroke at least 0.9 mm wide (two 0.4 mm perimeters) or it will not print — scale the text up rather than thinning it, and say in a comment what size you landed on.
TEXT: "{text}", {mode}, {depth} mm deep. Keep every stroke at least 0.9 mm wide or it will not print at a 0.4 mm nozzle.
TEXT: "{text}", {mode}, on the {where}. Use 0.6–1 mm depth and keep strokes at least 0.9 mm wide.
TEXT: "{text}", {mode}. Use 0.6–1 mm depth and keep every stroke at least 0.9 mm wide.
TEXT: the part carries the text "{text}". Engrave it 0.6–1 mm deep with strokes at least 0.9 mm wide.

tools.label: Strength
tools.hint: What it has to survive. Drives walls and orientation.

lines.text: STRENGTH: {duty}; the load runs {load}; walls {walls} mm. Orient the part so that load runs in the bed plane, never across layer lines, and say in a comment which face goes on the bed and why.

STRENGTH: {duty}; the load runs {load}. Orient the part so that load runs in the bed plane, never across layer lines, and say in a comment which face goes on the bed. Thicken walls and add fillets at the loaded root.
STRENGTH: {duty}; walls {walls} mm, as a named variable.
STRENGTH: {duty}. Size the walls and fillets for that, and state the assumption in a comment.
STRENGTH: the load runs {load}. Orient so that direction lies in the bed plane, and say which face goes down.
STRENGTH: walls {walls} mm, as a named variable.

tools.label: Material
tools.hint: Filament and environment. Changes clearances and geometry.

lines.text: MATERIAL: {filament}, used {where}. Account for it: PETG and TPU need larger clearances than PLA on mating faces; anything outdoors or hot must not be PLA and the geometry should not rely on it staying stiff. Say in one comment how the material changed a number.
MATERIAL: {filament}. PETG and TPU need larger mating clearances than PLA — adjust and say so in a comment.
ENVIRONMENT: this lives {where}. Do not assume PLA, and design the geometry so it does not depend on the part staying perfectly stiff.

tools.label: Print settings
tools.hint: Nozzle, layers, supports — the constraints the geometry must respect.

lines.text: PRINTING: {nozzle} mm nozzle, {layer} mm layers, {supports}. Every wall and every raised or cut detail must be a whole multiple of the nozzle width, and no unsupported overhang may exceed 45° unless supports were allowed.
PRINTING: {nozzle} mm nozzle, {supports}. Make every wall a whole multiple of the nozzle width, and keep overhangs under 45° unless supports were allowed.
PRINTING: {nozzle} mm nozzle, {layer} mm layers. Make every wall a whole multiple of the nozzle width.
PRINTING: {supports}. Keep unsupported overhangs under 45° and say in a comment which face goes on the bed.
PRINTING: {nozzle} mm nozzle. Make every wall a whole multiple of that width.
PRINTING: {layer} mm layers.

tools.label: Quantity
tools.hint: A set, arranged on one plate.

lines.text: QUANTITY: {count} of these. Expose the count as a variable and arrange that many copies on the plate with a few millimetres between them, so one render is one print.
QUANTITY: {count} of these. Expose the count as a variable.

tools.label: Style
tools.hint: Form language. Steers the reference images, not the maths.

lines.text: STYLE: {form}, {finish} surface, in the spirit of {like}.
STYLE: {form}, {finish} surface.
STYLE: {form}, in the spirit of {like}.
STYLE: {form}.
STYLE: {finish} surface.
STYLE: in the spirit of {like}.

tools.label: Colour
tools.hint: The colour the checkpoint is tagged with, and the look of the previews.

lines.text: COLOUR: tag the model {name} so it reads clearly in the viewport.

tools.label: Mesh detail
tools.hint: How fine the generated mesh comes out. Costs time.
